manoj-kumar-sharma-12th-fail-ips-upsc-fo.seo_title: Manoj Kumar Sharma: UPSC rank, attempts and real 12th Fail story
manoj-kumar-sharma-12th-fail-ips-upsc-fo.answer: Manoj Kumar Sharma cleared the UPSC civil services exam on his fourth attempt with All India Rank 121. He is a 2005-batch IPS officer, Maharashtra cadre. He failed Class 12 in Morena, Madhya Pradesh, and the film 12th Fail is based on his life.
faq: Yes. The 2023 film is based on Anurag Pathak's book about IPS officer Manoj Kumar Sharma from Morena, Madhya Pradesh, who failed his Class 12 board exam and later cleared the civil services exam.
In which attempt did Manoj Kumar Sharma clear UPSC?
He cleared the civil services exam on his fourth attempt, with an All India Rank of 121, and joined the IPS in 2005 in the Maharashtra cadre.
What was Manoj Kumar Sharma's UPSC rank?
He cleared the UPSC Civil Services Examination with an All India Rank of 121 and joined the Indian Police Service (IPS).
Where is Manoj Kumar Sharma posted now?

In March 2024 he was promoted to Inspector General rank and appointed IG in the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF), on deputation from the Maharashtra cadre. Reports from 2024 place him in charge of CISF security at Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport. Postings change, so check a recent news report for his current role.
What jobs did Manoj Kumar Sharma do while preparing for UPSC?
He drove a tempo, worked in a library and walked dogs for families in Delhi to pay for coaching fees and books.
Why did Manoj Kumar Sharma fail Class 12?
Reports say copying was common in his area until a strict officer stopped it in the year of his exam, and he failed. He later cleared Class 12 on his second attempt.
Who is Manoj Kumar Sharma's wife?
His wife is Shraddha Joshi, whom he met while preparing for the civil services exam. She is an Indian Revenue Service officer.

dick-fosbury-flop-laughed-at-olympic-gol.answer: Dick Fosbury lent his name to the Fosbury Flop in the high jump. Going over the bar head-first and backwards, he won high-jump gold at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics with an Olympic-record 2.24 metres.

steven-spielberg-rejected-by-usc-film-sc.answer: No. USC's film school rejected Steven Spielberg twice. He studied at California State College, Long Beach, left in 1968 for a Universal contract, and finished his degree there in 2002, aged 55.

vera-wang-started-her-company-at-40-stor.answer: Vera Wang opened her first bridal salon in New York in 1990, at about 40. Before that she missed the 1968 U.S. Olympic skating team and spent 17 years at Vogue.

lijjat-papad-seven-women-80-rupees-story.seo_title: Lijjat Papad turnover 2026, founders and ₹80 start
lijjat-papad-seven-women-80-rupees-story.answer: Lijjat Papad's annual turnover is reported at more than ₹1,600 crore. Seven women in Girgaum, Mumbai, started it on 15 March 1959 with ₹80 borrowed money, and about 45,000 women now co-own it.

money.intro: To understand Lijjat's success, look at three numbers: the money it started with, how fast it grew, and what each member actually earns.
points: The ₹80 start: capital was never the advantage

Adjusted for India's consumer price inflation, the ₹80 the women borrowed in 1959 is worth roughly ₹7,400 today, less than many people spend on a phone. As an accountant, this is the number I keep coming back to. Lijjat was not built on money.
Compounding: the real engine of growth

Sales in the first year were just over ₹6,000. Reports now put turnover at about ₹1,600 crore, roughly 27 lakh times larger. That works out to sales growing about 26% a year, every year, for more than six decades, or about 18% a year after removing inflation. Very few Indian businesses of any kind have sustained that for so long.
Turnover is not profit: read the figure correctly

₹1,600 crore is shared across about 45,000 members. That is roughly ₹3.6 lakh of sales per member each year, before the cost of flour, spices and packing. Lijjat's real achievement is not one big number. It is thousands of steady, modest earnings that the women own outright.

First-year sales (just over ₹6,000), in today's money
Sales in 1962-63 (close to ₹2 lakh), in today's money
Growth from first-year sales to ₹1,600 crore
borrow: Start with what you have: a small amount spent on something people buy every week can be enough to begin.
Value consistency over speed: steady growth for decades beats one good year. Even 15% a year turns ₹1 lakh into about ₹66 lakh over 30 years.
Check the right number: when you read a company's turnover, ask what is left after costs and how many people share it.

ray-kroc-52-milkshake-mixer-salesman-bui.seo_title: How old was Ray Kroc when he met the McDonald brothers?
ray-kroc-52-milkshake-mixer-salesman-bui.answer: Ray Kroc was 52 when he met Dick and Mac McDonald in San Bernardino in 1954, while selling milkshake mixers. He opened his first McDonald's in 1955 and bought the brothers out for $2.7 million in 1961.

paras: In 1961 Ray Kroc paid the McDonald brothers $2.7 million for their rights, about $28 million in today's dollars. Before that deal, the brothers took just 0.5% of their franchisees' sales. That is a small share of a fast-growing business, and Kroc's own cut was only 1.4%.

The money was really made in property. Harry Sonneborn's plan had the company own or lease the land and rent it to franchisees, so rent arrived every month whatever happened to burger prices. When McDonald's listed in 1965 at $22.50 a share, about $224 today, investors were buying a property business as much as a restaurant chain.

oldest-olympic-medal-winners-athletes-wh.answer: The oldest Olympic medallist is Sweden's Oscar Swahn, who won shooting silver at the 1920 Olympics aged 72. He is also the oldest gold medallist, at 64 in 1912.

marvel-bankruptcy-1996-to-disney-4-billi.seo_title: Marvel bankruptcy 1996: why it went bust and what saved it
marvel-bankruptcy-1996-to-disney-4-billi.answer: Marvel filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in December 1996 after the comics and trading-card boom collapsed. It merged with Toy Biz in 1998, financed its own films, made Iron Man in 2008, and Disney bought it for about $4 billion in 2009.

paras: In 1998 Marvel reportedly offered Sony almost all its film characters for $25 million, about $48 million in today's dollars. Eleven years later Disney paid about $4 billion for the company, 160 times that offer, or nearly $5.8 billion today.

What changed in between was not the characters but who kept the profit. Selling film rights for a fixed fee turns a character into a one-off payment. In 2005 Marvel instead borrowed $525 million against its remaining rights to make its own films. Iron Man earned about $585 million, roughly $850 million today, and that income went to Marvel.

ms-dhoni-ticket-collector-kharagpur-to-w.answer: Yes. MS Dhoni worked as a travelling ticket examiner for South Eastern Railway at Kharagpur, reportedly from 2001 to 2004. In 2011 he scored 91 not out in the World Cup final and hit the winning six.

sundar-pichai-slept-on-living-room-floor.seo_title: Sundar Pichai's childhood in Chennai: house, family, struggles
sundar-pichai-slept-on-living-room-floor.answer: Sundar Pichai grew up in a modest house in Chennai shared with tenants. His family slept on the living room floor, queued for water in a drought and waited five years for a phone.

jadav-payeng-forest-man-of-india-molai-f.seo_title: Molai forest: Jadav Payeng, the Forest Man of India (Assam)
jadav-payeng-forest-man-of-india-molai-f.answer: Jadav Payeng, the Forest Man of India, is from Assam. Since 1979 he has planted Molai forest on a Brahmaputra sandbar near Jorhat; it now covers about 1,360 acres (about 550 hectares).

sudha-murty-postcard-jrd-tata-telco-1974.answer: Yes. In 1974, after a TELCO job notice said lady candidates need not apply, she wrote a postcard to J.R.D. Tata asking how a company like TELCO could discriminate on the basis of gender. She tells the story in her piece "Appro JRD", published by Tata.

paras: The famous ₹10,000 sounds tiny, but 1981 prices were very different. Adjusted for inflation, it is worth about ₹2.1 lakh today. That is real savings for a young family, and Sudha Murty still kept ₹250 back for emergencies. That habit tells you more about how Infosys was run than the headline number does.

The growth is the real lesson. In 1999, the year it listed on Nasdaq, Infosys crossed US$100 million in revenue. It now reports about US$20 billion, roughly 200 times more. That is about 23% growth a year for 26 years, at a company already large when the run began.

paras: Sunil Mittal's ₹20,000 from 1976 is worth about ₹6.3 lakh in today's money. That is a serious sum for an 18-year-old, but it is roughly what a small trader might put into a shop today, not venture capital.

As an accountant, what stands out is that it was borrowed, from his father. Borrowed money has to come back, which forces a business to sell something early. A bicycle-parts workshop does exactly that: small, steady orders that pay the loan, long before anything as ambitious as a phone network.
money.note: Inflation uses India's consumer price index from the World Bank (series FP.CPI.TOTL, to 2025). Figures are rounded. General education, not financial advice.

sunil-bharti-mittal-20000-rupees-ludhian.answer: In April 1976, at 18, he borrowed ₹20,000 and started a small business in Ludhiana making bicycle crankshafts for local bicycle manufacturers.
sunil-bharti-mittal-20000-rupees-ludhian.answer_q: How did Sunil Mittal start his business?

paras: Ronald Wayne's $800 from 1976 is worth about $4,400 in today's dollars. Including the later $1,500, he received $2,300, about $12,700 today. Set against estimates of more than $400 billion for a 10% stake now, it looks like the worst trade in history.

The accountant's view is different. In a general partnership, each partner can be personally liable for the business's debts. Jobs had just borrowed $15,000 for parts, about $83,000 today, and Wayne had a house and savings that creditors could reach. He was not selling a share of Apple's future. He was buying protection from a debt he could not control.

At its first close as a public company in 2020, Airbnb was worth about $86.5 billion, roughly 58,000 times that 2008 valuation. As an accountant I would add one caution: early shares get diluted by every later funding round, so a 10% stake would have shrunk well before 2020. It would still have been worth billions.

paras: After Nvidia launched CUDA in 2006, its costs rose while revenue stood still, and its market value fell from about $12 billion to roughly $2 to $3 billion. Investors were treating the extra cost as waste.

On 29 October 2025 Nvidia closed at about $5.03 trillion, roughly 2,000 times its low point. In accounting terms, CUDA was spending that looked like an expense for years but behaved like an investment. The balance sheet could not show its value until the market for AI chips arrived.

paras: Netflix's asking price in 2000 was $50 million, about $91 million in today's dollars. Blockbuster had about $6 billion of annual revenue, so the price was less than 1% of one year's sales.

But price is not the only number an accountant looks at. Netflix expected to lose about $57 million that year, more than its own asking price. Buying it meant taking on those losses as well. The deal looked expensive on the profit and loss account and cheap only in hindsight.

Two decades later, in 2016, the company raised about ₹451 crore in its share issue at ₹321 a share. The shares opened about 5% below that price. A modest first day does not change the underlying story: a repair shop that started with ₹15,000 became a listed company.

paras: In 2025-26 the Amul brand's turnover crossed ₹1 lakh crore. Spread across about 36 lakh farmer-owners, that is roughly ₹2.8 lakh of sales for each farmer family, though it is turnover, not profit.

The federation's own turnover rose from ₹65,911 crore to ₹73,450 crore, about 11% in a year. Even the film Manthan (1976) was paid for by about five lakh farmers giving ₹2 each. That ₹2 is worth about ₹63 today, and the total of about ₹10 lakh would be about ₹3.1 crore.

paras: PhysicsWallah's first outside round, in June 2022, valued it at $1.1 billion. By September 2024 it was valued at $2.8 billion, about 2.5 times higher in just over two years.

Its share issue then raised about ₹3,480 crore at ₹109 a share. For an accountant, the interesting part is the order: years of free YouTube lessons built the audience first, and paid courses came later. The audience was the asset, even though it never appeared on a balance sheet.

paras: In 1969 Nirma sold at ₹3 a kilo when the cheapest rival cost ₹13. In today's money that is about ₹160 against about ₹690. Nirma was about 77% cheaper.

A price that low only works with very low costs. Patel made the powder himself, had no shop and no advertising at first, and sold door to door by bicycle while keeping his day job. As an accountant, I see a business that kept its overheads near zero until sales could carry them.

karsanbhai-patel-nirma-detergent-3-rupee.answer: Karsanbhai Patel (also spelled Karshanbhai Patel), a chemistry graduate who worked as a lab technician in Gujarat, started Nirma in 1969 by making detergent powder in his backyard near Ahmedabad.

paras: Facebook's 2014 deal was worth up to $19 billion for WhatsApp, which had more than 450 million monthly users. That is about $42 for each user.

Only $4 billion, about 21%, was cash. About $12 billion was Facebook shares, and $3 billion was restricted stock for founders and staff that they had to stay to earn. As an accountant, I would say the headline number tells you the value. The mix of cash and shares tells you how much risk the sellers took on.

paras: Glitch cost about $17 million to develop, about $24 million in today's dollars, and it failed. The chat tool the team built for themselves while making it became Slack.

In December 2020 Salesforce agreed to pay $27.7 billion, about 1,600 times what Glitch cost. That was also about 69 times Slack's yearly revenue of around $400 million. Accountants would call Glitch a sunk cost, but here the cost bought a tool nobody had planned to sell.

paras: Phil Knight's $50 from his father is worth only about $500 in today's dollars. His first year of sales, about $8,000, would be about $81,000 today. It was a side business run from a car boot, not a company.

The Swoosh logo cost $35 in 1971, about $270 today, possibly the best-value design fee ever paid. By 2016 Nike's yearly sales topped $30 billion. The early years show a familiar pattern: sales grew, but the business kept running short of cash, because growing a stock business ties money up in shoes before customers pay.

Instagram had no revenue at all. Facebook was paying for users and growth, not for profits. The founders' $500,000 seed round in 2010, about $720,000 today, bought a stake in something worth over a thousand times more within two years.

Britannica estimates he was earning about $300,000 a year from it by then. So the price was under seven years of his income, plus a salary. For a man in his seventies, swapping uncertain future earnings for cash and a guaranteed income was a reasonable choice.

For a teacher earning a modest salary, that difference was life-changing. King said he realised he would not have to teach any more. An advance is a prepayment against future royalties; the paperback sale showed what the book was actually worth to the market.
